How Big Water is trying to stop the National Park Service from cleaning up plastic bottles that are fouling the parks

A bit misleading title, they are trying to prevent the ban of selling bottled water. I don't mind a ban though, I always hike with sport bottles and the easily accessible parts of America's national parks are quite littered by disposable plastic bottles.

Would it really impact me (personally) if they stopped selling bottled water in the parks? Of course not; I'd just bring my own. However, I am always concerned when I see government passing laws and regulations that are not well thought-out, don't really solve the problem, and cause significant unintended consequences.

For example, have you ever driven to the southern rim of the grand canyon? People will simply turn around and drive 5 miles back to Tusayan where a gas station is more than happy to sell overpriced bottled water to tourists. Or, they will bring their own bottled water bottles and throw them "into" the overflowing garbage cans or along the trails.

People who currently litter will simply continue to litter. And poor management will continue to poorly manage certain parks. The only significant difference is that the gas station 5 miles south of the southern Grand Canyon will collect all the profits. Surely the profits from $2-3 16oz bottels of water more than cover the costs of paying garbage collectors and even staff to walk the paths every few days and pick up trash.

That begs an interesting question: Since the Nat Park Service isn't currently using the existing bottled water profits to empty the trash or clean the trails on a regular basis, what exactly are they using the profits for...and what plan do they have to fund those activities after the profits from bottled water bottles is shifted to surrounding gas stations and mini-marts? Should we be surprised that the Parks will soon be complaining about the need to raise the park fees (or threaten to cut other services) because the bottled water profits were shifted to the gas stations down the road?

What a joke. A better solution? Just empty the garbage cans on a regular basis. That was not very complicated and will now free up the National Park Service to worry about more important things like what a shitshow the National Mall is in DC.

I visit every year and EVERY time for the past 5 years, the grass is half dead/brown with big sections of mud everywhere, the garbage cans are overflowing (ALL DAY LONG), the fountains are mostly broke and drained. The reflecting pool was a fucking disgusting moldy/algae/stinky mess for years...although they may have finally addressed that issue this year. It's a national embarrassment.

It's almost as if that organization does everything is possibly can to defect blame and attention from its shitty management.

I've really gotten into KSP over the last few weeks. I have an X52 Pro and started out using Windows because I didn't think it would be supported on Linux. I ended up running into the bug where there was some significant lag in input time, and button presses frequently repeated themselves (think how annoying it is to push your stage button and have it go off twice). The whole experience was frustrating, not to mention the fact that I had already spent a lot of time getting drivers installed for the X52 that actually worked because Saitek doesn't sign their drivers.

Then I remembered there's a Linux release. I had to make some adjustments to my system to get things working (I'm on gentoo and hadn't enabled joystick support in the kernel yet). I used qjoypad which was a nice, simple, useful way to bind keypresses to buttons on my joystick (KSP freaks out in Windows and Linux when it sees more than 20 buttons). The only issue I have is vsync doesn't work but I think that's something wrong with my system specifically, like I said I use gentoo and I believe I've simply misconfigured something somewhere as this happens in other games.

In the end I found using Linux was way easier (even on my hacked up Gentoo installation, don't get me wrong, I love it) and I had a noticeable performance increase when using the 64 bit version over what I had seen on Windows. I consider this a big win for gaming on Linux for me.

Edit: just wanted to mention I'm a software engineer in real life and use Linux every day in some way. I'd love to see the day when a relatively mainstream game is released for Linux and NOT Windows. Also if you'd like to set up KSP on Linux with an X52 Pro and are having trouble PM me and I'll be glad to help you out.

[After the siege of Khmun]

A short while later, the city capitulated and its treasuries were emptied for Piankhie - even Nimlot's [the Libyan ruler of Khmun] royal crown was offered up as a trophy. In a pathetic gesture of submission, the defeated leader's female relatives came to beg mercy from Piankhi's wives, daughters, and sisters - a plea for clemency, woman to woman. Nimlot's own act of obeisance was to appear before his nemesis with two well-chosen gifts: a sistrum made of gold and lapis lazuli, used in temple rituals to appease a deity, and a horse. Like every other Kushite ruler, Piankhi was a lover of all things equine. (He was so pleased with the gifts, and the gesture, that he had them immortalized in stone at the top of his victory monument, erected on his return home in the temple of Amun at Gebel Barkal.)

Piankhi's fondness for horses showed itself again in an extraordinary episode some hours later, when he went to inspect Nimlot's palace. Two rooms in particular caught his eye, the treasury and the stables. What followed speaks volumes about Piankhi's priorities:

The king's [Nimlot's] wives and daughters came to him and paid honor to him as women do. But His Majesty did not pay them any attention. Instead, he went off to the stables, where he saw that the horses were hungry. He said... "It is more painful to me that my horses should be hungry than every other ill deed you have done!"

The Nubian pharaoh would not be the last monarch in history to prefer horses to people.

Source:

Wilkinson, Toby A. H. "A Tarnished Throne." The Rise and Fall of Ancient Egypt. New York: Random House, 2010. 395, 396. Print.
